name: Verdicchio

lines.s10: Verdicchio is the lemony white of the Marche on Italy's Adriatic coast, sharp and fresh, with a firm finish of bitter almond.
lines.s20: Verdicchio grows in the hills of the Marche, behind the Adriatic port of Ancona. It is a dry white with high acidity, and it tastes of lemon, green apple and fennel, ending on a clean bitterness of almond.
lines.s45: Verdicchio comes from the Marche, from the hills behind the Adriatic port of Ancona, and it is that coast's white for fish. It tastes of lemon, green apple and fennel, and it ends on a clean bitterness of almond. It is dry and medium in body, with high, bright acidity. Most is bottled young from steel tanks. A Riserva rests longer, and over ten years it turns to honey and toasted almond. It belongs with fried seafood, raw fish or a fish stew. In the 1950s it was given a green bottle shaped like an amphora, and that bottle carried its name round the world.
lines.sale: When the plate is sharp, salty or fried, Verdicchio holds its ground: bright lemon, high acidity and a firm finish of bitter almond. Have it with the shrimp remoulade or the fried seafood.

glass.lead: Lemon, green apple and wild fennel on high, bright acidity, dry and medium in body, closing on bitter almond and a salty edge.

ladder.where: Matelica, a high inland valley closed to the sea
The Castelli di Jesi, nearer the Adriatic, and Lugana

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, alcohol medium to medium plus, body medium, with a faintly oily feel and a firm, bitter almond finish.

home.home: The Marche, on Italy's Adriatic coast. Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, in the hills west of Ancona, is the larger and broader zone; Verdicchio di Matelica, in a high inland valley, is leaner and slower to open. Both hold at least 85 per cent Verdicchio and are made mostly in steel, and the Riserva of each ages for years.
home.abroad: It hardly leaves Italy. In the Veneto it is Trebbiano di Soave, a minor partner in Soave, and on the clay shore of Lake Garda its near twin, Turbiana, makes Lugana, typically a little rounder.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; an aged Riserva a few degrees warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass; a wider bowl for an aged Riserva.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary. A closed Riserva may gain from a few minutes of air in the glass.
service.age: Most within three years; a Riserva from Jesi or Matelica keeps ten years or more, gaining honey and toasted almond.

labels.means: The larger zone, in the hills west of Ancona; Classico marks its historic core.
The smaller zone, a high inland valley: leaner, sharper and slower to open.
Longer aged, at least eighteen months, and since 2010 a DOCG of its own in each zone.
The Lake Garda white and its grape, once called Trebbiano di Lugana; DNA study ties it to Verdicchio.
Verdicchio's name in the Veneto, a minor partner to Garganega in Soave; a different vine from Trebbiano Toscano.

guest.q: I like Sauvignon Blanc. Will I like Verdicchio?
guest.a: I think so. It has the same brisk acidity and lemon, but it is quieter in scent, with fennel and bitter almond where Sauvignon Blanc has gooseberry and cut grass.

guest.q: Can an Italian white like this really age?
guest.a: This one can. Its high acidity keeps it fresh, and a Riserva from a good year moves from lemon and green apple to honey, beeswax and toasted almond over ten years or more.

guest.q: The list has a Lugana. Is that the same grape?
guest.a: As near as makes no difference. Lugana, from the clay shore of Lake Garda, is made from Turbiana, which DNA study ties to Verdicchio. It tends to be a little rounder and gentler.

compare.tell: Garganega, as Soave, is softer and rounder, with white peach and gentler acidity; Verdicchio is leaner and sharper, with lemon, fennel and green almond.
Trebbiano Toscano is a different vine, lighter and plainer; Verdicchio has more flavour and a bitter almond finish. Trebbiano di Soave is Verdicchio; Trebbiano di Lugana its near twin.
Fiano is broader and waxier, with ripe pear, honeysuckle and hazelnut; Verdicchio is leaner and higher in acidity, with lemon and a bitter almond finish.

profile.st: Pale straw with green glints · Body medium · Acid high · Alcohol medium to medium plus · Dry, with a firm, faintly bitter finish
profile.fruit: Lemon zest, green apple; yellow apple from the riper sites of the Castelli di Jesi
profile.other: Wild fennel and anise, bitter and green almond, struck flint and a salty edge; honey, beeswax and toasted almond with age; mostly no oak
profile.tell: High acidity with lemon, fennel and a firm bitter almond finish on a medium body, a green glint in the colour: Verdicchio from the Marche
profile.regions: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi and Verdicchio di Matelica in the Marche; Lugana on Lake Garda, as Turbiana; Soave, as Trebbiano di Soave
profile.confuse: Garganega is softer, with white peach; Fiano is broader and waxier, with hazelnut; Trebbiano Toscano is lighter and plainer; Vermentino is saltier and softer in acidity, with lime and thyme

cards.front: Verdicchio: name its two zones in the Marche and how they differ.
cards.back: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, in the hills west of Ancona, is larger and broader. Verdicchio di Matelica, in a high inland valley closed to the sea, is leaner, sharper and slower to open.

cards.front: What do Trebbiano di Soave and Turbiana have to do with Verdicchio?
cards.back: One is its other name, the other its near twin. DNA study ties Verdicchio to Trebbiano di Soave in the Veneto and to Turbiana, the grape of Lugana on Lake Garda. Neither is Trebbiano Toscano.

cards.front: Verdicchio blind: what gives the glass away?
cards.back: A green glint, high acidity, lemon, green apple and fennel on a medium body, and a firm finish of bitter almond. With age it gains honey and toasted almond.

questions.q: A blind Italian white is pale straw with a green glint, dry and medium in body, with high acidity, lemon, green apple and fennel, no oak and a firm finish of bitter almond. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: High acidity with lemon, fennel and a firm bitter almond finish points to Verdicchio. Garganega shares the almond but is softer, with white peach; Arneis is soft in acidity, and Fiano is broader and waxier.

questions.q: A guest enjoyed a Lugana beside Lake Garda and asks for a wine of the same grape from its home on the Adriatic side of Italy. Which do you bring?
questions.exp: Lugana is made from Turbiana, which DNA study ties to Verdicchio, the grape of the Marche. Trebbiano d'Abruzzo tempts because Turbiana was once called Trebbiano di Lugana, but it is made from other vines.

questions.q: A guest wants a Verdicchio with some years behind it, turned to honey and toasted almond, to pour with roast rabbit and mushrooms. Which word on the label do you look for?
questions.exp: Riserva marks the longer aged wine, a DOCG in each zone since 2010. Classico names the historic core of the Jesi zone and says nothing of age, and Passito is a sweet wine from dried grapes.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: the Marche, with Soave and Lugana given as abroad, since the grape hardly leaves Italy.

A new grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the four targets are the Marche, Lombardy, the Veneto and Italy, whose records already name Verdicchio, Turbiana or Trebbiano di Soave.

No Codex record is contradicted. The Codex already holds Verdicchio as the Marche's white, named for its green tinge, high in acid, with lemon, green apple, fennel, almond and a bitter almond finish, honey, beeswax and toasted almond with age; the two zones at 85 per cent, Matelica leaner and slower to open; the Riserva of each a DOCG since 2010; steel, lees and some large old cask; the amphora shaped bottle that carried it abroad after the Second World War; brodetto, fried seafood and crudo, and the Riserva with white meats and mushrooms.
Say: the Codex holds two respellings, ver-DEEK-kyoh in the Marche record and ver-DEEK-kee-oh in the Italy record. The entry takes the first, which is nearer the Italian.

A doubt on a Codex record, for the owner: the Lombardy and Marche records state that Lugana's Turbiana is Verdicchio, the same variety. Sources read agree that DNA study ties them, but the Lugana consortium treats Turbiana as a vine of its own and later work describes it as a biotype, almost identical. The entry says DNA study ties it to Verdicchio, which both readings allow, and the Lugana rules themselves name the grape as Trebbiano di Soave, locally Turbiana or Trebbiano di Lugana.

The Riserva at eighteen months, six of them in bottle, stands on the production rules and on several pages that restate them; one page read gives 24 months and is taken as an error. Only the eighteen months is written.
The amphora bottle is dated to the 1950s (sources give 1953); the house that commissioned it and the architect who drew it are not named, by the house rules.

Lugana as a little rounder than the Marche wines is a taster's reading, hedged with typically and tends to; the Codex's Lombardy record gives it weight from white clay, medium body, citrus, almond and a saline edge.
Lemon pith, yellow apple, anise, green almond, struck flint and sea salt are a taster's naming around the notes the Codex gives (lemon, green apple, fennel, almond, flint, a saline bite).

Left out for want of a second source: plantings outside Italy, the years the two DOCs were first granted (sources give 1967 for Matelica and 1968 for Jesi, one source each here), the sparkling and passito versions as label terms, and any parentage.
Shrimp remoulade is the one dish from the Creole table: high acidity and lemon against a sharp, mustard sauce.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The two zones at 85 per cent, the Riserva of each at eighteen months and a DOCG, the green amphora bottle of 1953, Verdicchio as one vine with Trebbiano di Soave and its tie to Lugana's Turbiana were confirmed.
changed: profile.confuse: Vermentino is saltier, with lime and wild herbs carried a family word dressed up, and fennel, the herb a taster would name first, is Verdicchio's own note. It now reads saltier and softer in acidity, with lime and thyme, as the Vermentino entry gives them.
questions[2].q: honeyed and nutty, two family words in the guest's mouth, now read turned to honey and toasted almond, the notes the entry gives an aged Riserva.

compare, Trebbiano: old labels of Trebbiano di Soave or di Lugana made both names things of the past. Trebbiano di Soave is the name the Soave rule still uses; only Trebbiano di Lugana has given way to Turbiana. The line now reads Trebbiano di Soave, and the old Trebbiano di Lugana, are Verdicchio.
open: Turbiana: the Vitis study of 2001 found Verdicchio identical with Trebbiano di Soave and very similar to Trebbiano di Lugana; a later study found one profile across its samples, a Turbiana among them; a still later account says the two are not identical, which is why Lugana took the name Turbiana. The entry says DNA study ties them, which every reading allows, and its second card calls both names Verdicchio's own, as the Codex's records do.
Whether the Matelica Riserva must spend six of its eighteen months in bottle, as the Jesi Riserva must: two pages read disagree. The entry states only the eighteen months.
One shop note read finds Matelica the more scented of the two zones, with apricot. The entry keeps the Codex's leaner, sharper Matelica.
